Phase 2 · Security analysis and selection

Select investments the client can actually own

Translate the approved allocation into a focused candidate set, use funds and ETFs as the primary vehicles, and build an intentional portfolio of 8–10 holdings—never more than 10.

Stop before research

If a client guardrail or information gap is missing, return to the Phase 1 decision record. A product search cannot repair an incomplete mandate.

Step 1 · Candidate pool and boundaries

Set the candidate pool and portfolio boundaries

Translate each approved allocation sleeve and client mandate into a short candidate pool with plausible alternatives. Separate must-pass constraints from preferences, and do not research only the team's preferred product.

Holding count and vehicle mix

Target 8–10 final holdings per client portfolio and never exceed 10. Eight is a valid complete portfolio; do not add a holding merely to fill a slot.

Funds and ETFs are the primary implementation vehicles. Individual securities are permitted only when they add a distinct, mandate-aligned benefit and are limited to two or three total per portfolio. Individual bonds are not required.

  • Every holding has a distinct purpose in the portfolio and fits the approved client mandate.
  • The holding adds useful exposure or diversification without unnecessary duplication or concentration.
  • The position and its underlying exposure have liquidity appropriate to the client and the planned weight.
  • The holding's cost, trading expenses, risks, and implementation demands are proportionate to its benefit.

Step 2 · Shared final-holding analysis

Complete one scorecard per final holding

Every fund, ETF, and individual security uses the same seven core tests. The instrument add-ons in Step 3 supply only evidence that is not already captured here.

One shared final-holding scorecard and decision record. Complete one row for each final holding, not every screened name.
Candidate and instrument typeRole ownerApproved allocation sleeve and Phase 1 guardrailPortfolio exposure and roleCost and trading expensesLiquidityHoldings, sector, and style overlapDiversification contributionKey risks and bear-case sensitivityClient-mandate fitIndividual-security rationale, idiosyncratic risk, and position size if applicableVerified source and as-of dateFinal select/reject decision, concise alternative rejected, and key trade-off

Individual-security add-on

  • Why an individual security is superior to a fund or ETF for this specific role
  • Idiosyncratic risk
  • Position-size rationale and concentration limit

Rejected alternatives

Compare the strongest realistic alternatives and record why they were rejected in one concise decision record. Full scorecards are required for final holdings, not every screened name.

AI challenge and human verification

Record the provisional leader before asking AI for the strongest counterargument or missing risk. Verify every material claim with an approved source, then record Accept, Modify, or Reject and explain what changed. AI is not a source and may not choose the product for the team.

Step 3 · Instrument add-ons and role handoff

Add only evidence that is unique to the instrument

Do not restate cost, liquidity, overlap, diversification, client fit, rejected alternatives, or trade-offs here—the shared scorecard already captures them.

Lead: Fixed-Income Analyst

Fixed-income fund, ETF, or limited direct exposure

Does the exposure fit the client's income, capital-preservation, duration, credit, liquidity, tax, and rate-risk guardrails?

Add only

  • Yield or income measure and its return drivers under the base and bear macro cases
  • Duration or interest-rate sensitivity and the effect of a rate move
  • Credit quality, spread, and downgrade or default risk
  • Income-distribution and tax characteristics; use direct-bond terms only if a direct bond is actually proposed

Lead: Equity Analyst

Equity fund or ETF

Does the vehicle deliver the intended equity exposure efficiently without hidden concentration, overlap, trading, liquidity, tax, or style problems?

Add only

  • Objective, benchmark or index methodology, style, sector, region, and active or passive approach
  • Performance or tracking context using comparable periods and current as-of dates
  • Turnover, distributions, and tax implications
  • Any underlying issuer that is material enough to trigger the limited look-through review below

Lead: Equity Analyst

Limited individual equity

Does this individual security add a mandate-aligned benefit that a fund or ETF cannot provide without creating excessive idiosyncratic or concentration risk?

Add only

  • Business and return drivers, valuation context where relevant, and base/bear sensitivity
  • The three individual-security additions in the shared scorecard above
  • The concise Issuer Reality Check below

Role decision rights and handoff

Owned work

Client and Macro Strategist

Own the mandate screen: approve or reject candidate fit against the client's ranked goals, constraints, and base/bear macro scenarios.

Owned work

Fixed-Income Analyst

Recommend fixed-income finalists and add the income, duration, credit, tax, and rate-risk evidence that is unique to that sleeve.

Owned work

Equity Analyst

Recommend equity finalists and add benchmark or index, tracking, turnover, tax, and limited individual-equity evidence where applicable.

Owned work

Portfolio Manager

Integrate the finalists, resolve overlap and concentration, set the final 8–10 holdings and weights, and record rejected recommendations and portfolio trade-offs.

Owned work

Risk and Derivatives Analyst

Challenge risk estimates and data comparability, identify the residual risk to stress next, and own one targeted hedge or a fully supported no-hedge conclusion only after portfolio testing.

Residual-risk handoff

Security selection identifies the residual exposures to test; it does not manufacture a hedge. In the next workflow, the Risk and Derivatives Analyst stress-tests the integrated portfolio and documents either a fully supported no-hedge conclusion or at most one targeted hedge that addresses an identified residual risk.

Step 4 · Conditional issuer review

Issuer Reality Check—only when triggered

Decision rule

Yield or recent return alone cannot support a recommendation. The committee must evidence the issuer's financial health, operating outlook, and relevance to the client's mandate.

Always required

Direct individual security

Required for every direct individual security.

Conditional only

Fund or ETF look-through

For a fund or ETF, complete only a limited look-through review when one holding or issuer is material to the exposure, concentration, or risk conclusion. If no issuer is material to that conclusion, the shared holding scorecard is sufficient.

Five-field issuer snapshot

  1. Security, issuer, exposure type, portfolio weight, source, and as-of date
  2. Business model, principal revenue drivers, and industry or macro sensitivity under the base and bear cases
  3. Revenue, margin, cash-flow, liquidity, and leverage trend using consistent periods; include interest coverage and debt-maturity considerations where relevant
  4. One issuer-specific risk and the evidence that makes it material
  5. Conclusion about mandate fit and the effect on selection, weight, or monitoring

Return the conclusion to the shared scorecard

The analyst adds only the material issuer conclusion to the shared scorecard. The Portfolio Manager applies it to selection and weight; the Risk and Derivatives Analyst carries any residual issuer or concentration risk into portfolio stress testing and the hedge/no-hedge conclusion.

This conditional review is part of the holding's scorecard—not a second security-analysis assignment. Keep it concise, cited, and decision-focused.

Required licensed-source research

FactSet Research and Evidence Record

Public/private data boundary

Use your licensed FactSet access to research and download data for your own course work. Submit the final project package and any required licensed-source supporting evidence privately through Canvas. Do not place FactSet captures, exports, credentials, completed proprietary data files, or student work in the public repository.

FactSet layouts, entitlements, and labels can differ. Use course demonstrations and current FactSet support for navigation; this public guide defines the evidence standard, not a click path.

1

Frame the research question

Name the client guardrail, issuer claim, product comparison, or portfolio-risk input the FactSet research must test.

2

Retrieve licensed evidence

Research the relevant security, issuer, credit, financial-statement, fund/ETF, benchmark, holdings, or portfolio-risk data available in your licensed workspace.

3

Record the retrieval

Log what was retrieved, retrieval date, relevant metric or research item, entity/security, as-of period, and source or document reference as appropriate.

4

Interpret

Explain what the evidence means for return drivers, risk, issuer health, product exposure, diversification, or client fit. Do not substitute copied output for analysis.

5

Apply and retain

State how the evidence confirmed, qualified, contradicted, or changed the recommendation, then retain and submit the required licensed-source evidence privately through Canvas under course policy.

Conditional issuer review

For a direct individual security, or a fund/ETF holding that is material to the exposure, concentration, or risk conclusion, use current issuer evidence to complete only the concise Issuer Reality Check.

Credit and fixed income

Use relevant issue and issuer evidence for price/yield context, maturity and structure, duration or rate sensitivity, credit quality, spreads, liquidity, coverage, debt maturities, and downside risk.

Mutual funds and ETFs

Use relevant product, holdings, benchmark, style, performance, flow, risk, cost, liquidity, and overlap evidence while verifying official product facts in sponsor or filed documents when appropriate.

Portfolio risk inputs

Use appropriately dated risk, return, exposure, correlation, or benchmark inputs and document their definitions, units, limitations, and role in the team calculation.

FactSet Research and Evidence Log. Record the retrieval and interpretation; submit required licensed-source evidence privately through Canvas, never the public repository.

Selection gate

Ready to enter the portfolio?

  • Each portfolio has 8–10 purposeful final holdings, never more than 10; funds and ETFs are primary, individual securities total no more than two or three, and individual bonds are not required.
  • Every final holding completes the one shared scorecard; only applicable instrument-specific and individual-security add-ons are attached, and the strongest realistic alternative is rejected concisely.
  • The team excludes candidates that duplicate exposure, create unnecessary concentration, lack appropriate liquidity, or fail the client mandate, and uses approved sources and current as-of dates for material claims.
  • Every direct individual security has a concise Issuer Reality Check; a fund or ETF receives limited look-through only when an issuer is material to the exposure, concentration, or risk conclusion.
  • Each recommendation has a FactSet retrieval and interpretation record, while licensed evidence, proprietary exports, credentials, and student work remain private and are submitted through Canvas under course policy.
  • The AI challenge tests the provisional leader, material claims are verified with approved evidence, and the team records Accept, Modify, or Reject.
  • Each analyst records the recommendation, alternative rejected, and key trade-off; the Portfolio Manager records integration decisions, and a second member reviews the evidence trail.
  • The selected mix is evaluated for portfolio-level overlap, diversification, and residual risk before the Risk and Derivatives Analyst documents a supported no-hedge conclusion or at most one targeted hedge in the next workflow.

Record the handoff

For every selected candidate, state its portfolio job, proposed weight range, risk contribution, client-fit condition, and monitoring or removal trigger.
